description: Team of three working on the Space Mission Design Game challenge. We build games and tools: C#/Unity, 3D art, AI and computer vision, including lunar crater detection from NASA data. Our plan: a playable mission game where players choose a landing site from real lunar data, budget fuel and mass, and face real mission-design trade-offs. We're a full team, but happy to connect with other Istanbul teams to share ideas.
summary:
ORBITAL is a mission-design game. The player is the engineer of an uncrewed probe going to lunar polar orbit. Instead of flying the rocket by hand, you design the mission: choose a science goal and budget, build the spacecraft from real subsystems (structure, propulsion, power, attitude control, communications, computers and five science instruments), build the launch vehicle around it, and set the mission plan.

A live dashboard tracks mass, power, budget, data, communications, time and delta-v, so every choice shows its effect on the rest of the mission. The game refuses to launch designs that are physically impossible or over budget, and it lets risky designs fly so the player can watch them fail: a probe that flies past the Moon, or one that loses power in the Moon's shadow. A report then explains the cause and the fix, and the player redesigns and flies again.

ORBITAL teaches why space missions succeed or fail, in plain language, using NASA data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

The player picks a mission (Ice Prospector, Landing Site Scout or Full Polar Survey; each has a different science goal and budget), then works through three build stages: Spacecraft, Rocket and Mission Plan. Parts are grouped by category and shown as cards with mass, cost and a plain description. A live 3D model of the vehicle updates as parts are fitted.

HOW IT WORKS

An engineering model written in C++ evaluates every design: launcher and spacecraft delta-v, thrust-to-weight, fairing fit, power generation, battery energy for the Moon's shadow, data storage and downlink, mission lifetime and cost. Results appear on a seven-row dashboard (green, amber, red) and in a design review written in plain words.

- MUST FIX items block the launch: a missing part, too little thrust, not enough delta-v to reach the Moon, a payload too heavy for the fairing, or a cost over budget.

- RISK items allow the launch. The player then watches the consequence in flight, for example a probe that cannot brake into lunar orbit, or one whose battery runs out in the Moon's shadow.

The flight view plays the mission from ignition to lunar orbit and years of operations, with telemetry, an orbit map and an attitude indicator. A report gives the phase reached, the score, the cause and the fix, and a Redesign button returns the player to the builder with the same design.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

ORBITAL is for students and anyone curious about spaceflight, with no prior knowledge needed. It shows that mission design is a set of trade-offs: more instruments mean more mass, power, data and cost. There is no single correct design, and several different designs can succeed. Failure is treated as information: the player learns the reason, not only the result. The game is available in English and Turkish.

TOOLS

Unreal Engine 5.8 and C++. The engineering model, assembly rules, mission timeline and translation layer are plain C++ with automated tests. Git and GitHub for version control.

CREATIVITY

Most space games ask whether you can fly the rocket. ORBITAL asks whether you can design the mission. The two kinds of "no" (cannot launch, and launches then fails) mirror how real missions are reviewed and how they actually go wrong.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Plain language over jargon; honest limits (the model is simplified and educational, and its estimates are unsuitable for real flight planning); real NASA data for the Earth, the Moon, the stars and the launch audio; and no NASA logos or insignia anywhere in the game.
